name: ACL Tear
seo_title: ACL Tear Treatment in North Palm Beach | First Rehab
seo_desc: ACL tear physical therapy in North Palm Beach: non-surgical rehab and prehab before surgery, one-on-one with your therapist. Call 561-624-4263.
lede: After an ACL tear, physical therapy helps calm the knee and rebuild strength and stability, whether you are managing without surgery or preparing for it.
what_it_is: The anterior cruciate ligament runs diagonally through the middle of your knee, connecting the thighbone to the shinbone. According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, its job is to keep the shinbone from sliding out in front of the thighbone. Injuries are graded from a mild stretch (grade 1) to a partial tear (grade 2) to a complete tear (grade 3), in which the knee becomes unstable.

The AAOS reports that ACL injuries affect more than 200,000 people in the United States each year and that female athletes are injured at 2 to 8 times the rate of males. Most tears happen without contact, during cutting, pivoting, sudden stops or awkward landings. Mayo Clinic lists soccer, basketball, football, volleyball, gymnastics and skiing as higher-risk sports. A direct blow to the knee can also tear the ligament.
symptoms: A loud pop or popping feeling at the moment of injury
Severe pain and difficulty continuing the activity
A feeling that the knee is unstable or gives out
Loss of full range of motion
causes: Sudden change of direction or slowing down quickly
Pivoting with the foot firmly planted
A direct blow or collision to the knee
Poor conditioning, muscle fatigue or faulty landing technique

how_therapy_helps.intro: The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons states that non-operative management is always an option and includes working with physical therapy. In a randomized trial in the New England Journal of Medicine (Frobell and colleagues, 2010), young active adults who began with structured rehabilitation and had the option of later reconstruction had similar two-year results to those who had early surgery, and more than half of them had not had reconstruction by two years. When surgery is planned, Mayo Clinic notes that physical therapy beforehand helps strengthen the knee.
methods: Early work to settle the knee and regain full straightening and bending, which the APTA lists among the first goals after injury and before surgery.
Progressive weight-bearing and non-weight-bearing exercises to rebuild thigh strength, which drops quickly after an ACL injury.
Balance, perturbation and movement-control drills. The APTA knee ligament guideline recommends pairing neuromuscular re-education with strengthening for knees with stability problems.
Coaching on how to land, stop and pivot with good hip and knee control, the same skills Mayo Clinic describes in ACL prevention programs.
If reconstruction is planned, we work on swelling, motion and quadriceps strength beforehand and keep your surgeon informed of your progress.
The APTA guideline says clinicians may use functional bracing for knees without an intact ACL, so we help you and your doctor weigh whether one fits your activities.

first_visit: We review how the injury happened, whether you felt a pop, and which activities you want to return to. Your therapist measures swelling, knee range of motion and quadriceps strength, and watches how you walk and bear weight. Gentle hands-on stability tests, such as the Lachman test, help show how the ligament is functioning. We also check hip and ankle strength and coordinate the plan with your physician or surgeon.
recovery: Recovery depends on the grade of the tear, any other injuries in the knee, and what you need the knee to do. Mayo Clinic notes that a non-surgical approach can work well for people without knee instability, including those with partial tears or lower activity demands. For athletes returning to cutting and pivoting sports after reconstruction, Mayo Clinic says it can take a year or more to return safely, and the APTA notes it may take over a year to regain the strength, stability and power to play. If you have surgery, your surgeon's protocol guides each phase.
self_care: Follow rest, ice, compression and elevation in the first days after the injury
Ice for about 20 minutes at a time, as often as every two hours, as Mayo Clinic suggests
Use crutches if walking is painful or the knee feels unstable
Avoid pivoting, cutting and jumping until the knee has been evaluated
Prop the leg on pillows when resting to help reduce swelling
see_a_doctor: A pop with rapid swelling after an injury, since Mayo Clinic advises prompt care because cartilage or meniscus may also be damaged
You cannot bear weight on the leg
The knee gives out or feels unstable
A visible deformity of the leg or knee after the injury
The knee is locked and will not straighten
Severe pain associated with an injury

faqs.q: Can you recover from an ACL tear without surgery?
faqs.a: Some people can. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons says non-operative management is always an option, and Mayo Clinic notes it can work well for people whose knee is not unstable, including partial tears and lower activity demands. In a 2010 New England Journal of Medicine trial, more than half of young active adults who started with structured rehabilitation had not had reconstruction two years later, and their results were similar to those who had early surgery.

faqs.q: Can you walk on a torn ACL?
faqs.a: Right after the injury, walking is often painful, and the American Physical Therapy Association notes the knee usually swells within minutes to hours. Once swelling settles, many people can walk in a straight line, but the knee may feel loose or give way with turning. Walking on an unstable knee can risk further damage, so it is worth having the knee evaluated before you return to sports.

Prehab is physical therapy before ACL surgery. The American Physical Therapy Association describes it as reducing swelling, increasing knee range of motion and strengthening the quadriceps before reconstruction, and Mayo Clinic notes that physical therapy before surgery helps strengthen the knee. Going into the operation with a calm, mobile, stronger knee gives you a better starting point for rehabilitation, which then follows your surgeon's protocol.

faqs.q: How long after an ACL tear can you return to sports?
faqs.a: For athletes who have reconstruction, Mayo Clinic says it generally takes a year or more before it is safe to return to play, and the American Physical Therapy Association notes it may take over a year to regain strength, stability and power. Without surgery, timing depends on whether the knee stays stable during sport-specific drills. Return is usually based on strength, hop and movement testing rather than the calendar alone.

faqs.q: Is a partial ACL tear treated differently from a full tear?
faqs.a: Often, yes. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons grades a partial tear as grade 2, where the ligament is stretched and loosened, while a grade 3 tear is complete and leaves the knee unstable. Mayo Clinic notes that non-surgical care can work well for partial tears. The plan depends on how stable your knee is and what you want to do, which your doctor and therapist assess together.

The risk can be reduced. The American Physical Therapy Association reports that an analysis of multiple studies found a 67% reduction in non-contact ACL injuries in females who took part in prevention programs. Those programs ran at least six weeks, two to three times per week, and included strengthening, balance and landing practice. Mayo Clinic also recommends core and hamstring strengthening and proper jumping and pivoting technique.

signOrSymptom: popping sensation in the knee at injury
loss of knee range of motion

notes_for_reviewer: ICD-10 S83.51 (Sprain of anterior cruciate ligament of knee) verified on icd10data.com; billable children are S83.511-, S83.512-, S83.519- with A/D/S encounter characters.
Incidence conflict: AAOS says more than 200,000 ACL injuries per year in the US; ChoosePT says about 150,000. The page uses the AAOS figure only.
Frobell 2010 (KANON): 121 young active adults; 23 of 59 in the rehab-plus-optional-delayed group had reconstruction, 36 did rehab alone (about 61%), hence 'more than half'.
The 67% prevention figure is quoted from ChoosePT, which attributes it to an analysis of multiple studies in females; check you are comfortable with the attribution.
Kept non-surgical and prehab focus; post-reconstruction rehab content belongs on acl-reconstruction-rehab and should be internally linked.
